newsitem.title: USA: U.S. toughens line on Taleban.
newsitem.headline: U.S. toughens line on Taleban.

text.p: The United States toughened its line Monday toward Afghanistan's Taleban militia, condemning their execution of a former president and stressing concerns over such issues as terrorism and narcotics.
Last Friday, the State Department seemed more inclined to accept that Taleban was now the power in Afghanistan and to give it the benefit of the doubt on how it might govern.

Then, the department said it hoped "the new authorities in Kabul will move quickly to restore order and security and to form a representative interim government that can begin the process of reconciliation nationwide."
It also held out the possibility of re-establishing full diplomatic ties with Afghanistan.
But Monday, spokesman Nicholas Burns said the Taleban does not have control over all of the country and it was not clear that they have established a functioning government in Kabul.
"The situation on the ground is quite murky," he said.
As for upgrading diplomatic ties with the country, Burns said there was no thought now being given to that prospect.

Although the United States maintains diplomatic ties with Afghanistan, it has not had an embassy there since 1989 due to civil war. And there has not been a U.S. ambassador in the country since 1979 when a former envoy was assisnated.

As for other concerns, Burns said: "We have consistently raised with all authorities in Afghanistan, and this includes the Taliban, issues of great concern to the United States: terrorism, narcotics, human rights including due process, and the treatment of women -- which is a major issue for the United States and we'll continue to raise those issues."

"The United States ... joins in the condemnation in the United Nations of the summary execution of (former President) Mr. Najibullah and his associates. We condemn those summary executions and we've been clear about that," he said.
Last week, the department said Najibullah's execution was "regrettable."
Burns stressed that the United States would judge the Taleban on their actions.

Two years after their formation, the Taleban, a one-time band of Islamic student vigilantes, captured Kabul with barely a shot fired on Friday and extended its power when fighters captured the stronghold of former Afghan government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, north of the Kabul, on Monday.
The Taleban has begun enforcing a purist brand of Islam that has struck fear into many educated people, especially women, in the Afghan capital.
